facts.text: A striga is created when a cursed person who was buried dies but their curse survives, causing them to rise years later as a monster.
A striga is small, thickset, and hunched, but supernaturally fast, agile, and strong, making it dangerous even to experienced fighters.
Strigas usually hunt at night and become more aggressive during a full moon, though some attack during daytime.
Strigas feed on the flesh and blood of humans and animals, preferring internal organs like the liver and heart for sustenance during lethargic periods.
The curse can be lifted from a striga by waiting at its burial site through the night until the third crowing of a rooster catches it outside its coffin, returning it to human form.
Draconids form a large order including true dragons, of which at least half a dozen species exist, and lesser draconids.
Conflicts between draconids and humans increased as human settlements expanded into draconid territory.
Lesser draconids include slyzards, forktails, and wyverns, which share scaly skin, bony plate armor, bat wings, and reptilian features with true dragons.
Lesser draconids have atrophied forelegs, with wyverns and forktails having none at all, but possess long flexible necks for fast striking attacks.
True dragons are larger than lesser draconids, with two pairs of well-developed legs, huge wings and tails, and greater intelligence and cunning.
Dragons universally love to collect gold, gemstones, and treasure, a trait reflected in countless legends.
Most dragon hunts are motivated by greed for treasure rather than genuine desire to eliminate a threat or gain fame.
Dragon subspecies are classified by color: rock, green, red, black, white, and golden dragons.
Rock dragons are the smallest dragon subspecies and have been hunted to near extinction.
Black dragons are the largest dragon breed, actually a very dark brown color despite their name.
White dragons live in the far North and are known only from tales of a few explorers who describe their scales as light gray or light blue.
The golden dragon, draconis aurum nobilis, is a semimythical creature said to have telepathic communication and shapeshifting abilities, including the power to take human form.
A golden dragon named Villentretenmerth confronted King Niedamir of Caingorn and his dragon hunters near Woefield, forcing them to retreat.
The confrontation involving Villentretenmerth was confirmed by multiple eyewitnesses, including two sorcerers and a witcher.
The arachas is an insectoid predator originally native to the far South that has spread north over a few decades, adapting to colder climates by hibernating in mud or forest beds.
The arachas has a chitinous carapace covering its trunk and limbs, with a vulnerable abdomen it protects using shells or hollow logs as makeshift armor.
The arachas ambushes prey by launching a long tendril from its maw to pull victims toward itself, and some subspecies use mimicry to surprise victims.
Endregas are insectoids that live in colonies divided into castes, including workers who tend cocoons and larvae, and warriors who defend the nest and hunt.
Endregas are highly territorial and will attack any creature that approaches their nests, and growing colonies can threaten nearby human settlements.
The koshchey is an artificially created monster resulting from magical experiments, resembling a giant chitinous arachnid several meters long with powerful spiked pincers.
A koshchey is created by magically stimulating the growth of a regular uropygid until it reaches enormous size, retaining the strength-to-size ratio of a normal arachnid.
Only two cases of creating a koshchey have ever been recorded, credited to sorcerers Cosimo Malaspina and his apprentice Alzur.
The renegade druid Ferengal created a koshchey to help his band of robbers ambush merchant caravans crossing Klamat Pass, halting trade on that route.
Golems are magical constructs made by sorcerers from stone, clay, or wood to perform designated tasks such as carrying loads or fighting.
A golem is typically animated by a magical stone called a golem heart placed in its chest.
Golems have no will of their own and can only follow their creator's simple instructions, but they compensate with supernatural resilience and strength.
Golems used as guardians may continue their duties even after their creator's death.
Genies are commonly misnamed lesser elemental creatures summoned from one of four elemental planes (earth, fire, water, air), while true genies are beings of nearly unstoppable power.
Lesser elemental servant creatures, though weaker than true genies, are still mortally dangerous and can be defeated only by highly skilled individuals.
In a folktale, the sorceress Yennefer tried to ensnare a genie in a magical net in the Redanian city of Rinde to use it against local officials who had criticized her lifestyle.
The genie Yennefer tried to control escaped her spells and destroyed a dozen buildings in Rinde before a witcher named Gerhard used a secret exorcism to banish it.
Nekkers are small, misshapen creatures that live in colonies in dark woods, damp gullies, and shadowy dales, connected by underground tunnels.
Nekkers communicate through screeches, grunts, and moans that some scholars theorize may be a primitive language.
Nekkers hunt in packs, ambushing prey from underground tunnels and mobbing cornered victims, though they often hesitate before attacking due to low individual courage.
Larger, more aggressive nekkers called nekker warriors are identifiable by colorful clay smeared on their snouts and often lead groups of smaller nekkers.
Trolls are huge, strong, but not very intelligent creatures that are surprisingly skilled at carpentry and stonemasonry, building resilient structures like bridges.
Trolls often live near bridges and demand tolls of provisions, livestock, or horses from travelers, sometimes eating travelers who have nothing to offer.
Some intelligent trolls make deals with nearby villages, maintaining bridges and even protecting peasants from bandits or predators in exchange for goods.
Trolls have largely abandoned man-eating habits over time and are now considered a primitive intelligent race rather than true monsters.
Wilder mountain trolls sometimes still attack travelers and harass villages, especially in early spring when winter food stores run low.
Relicts are creatures that predate the arrival of men, elves, dwarves, and gnomes into the world, and are often too rare or unique to fit standard taxonomy.

The leshen, also called the Forest One or Wood One, is a shapeshifter inhabiting ancient forests, able to take forms from a bark-skinned old man to a horned deer-skulled beast or various forest animals.
A leshen can command the forest and its creatures to aid it in battle, making it highly dangerous and earning it the title of lord of the forest.
In some regions, leshens are worshipped as nature deities under the names Kerun or Kernos, with communities sacrificing small game or birds to them.
Leshens are highly territorial, often treating armed intruders such as bandits or hunters as threats to be driven off or eliminated.
Fiends and chorts are large beasts with bulging fur-covered torsos, goat-like hind legs, and antlers (fiends) or curved ram-like horns (chorts).
Fiends rarely leave their deep forest lairs, but when they do, their size and aggression cause catastrophic damage to nearby regions.
Geralt of Rivia was already a famous folk hero known as the White Wolf before his later deeds affected the fates of kingdoms.
Geralt of Rivia was infamously known as the Butcher of Blaviken for killing several people in broad daylight in that town.
Geralt of Rivia first met Dandelion at a fete in Gulet, in the Kingdom of Aedirn, and the two became close friends who traveled together.

Geralt of Rivia and Dandelion's first adventure together involved a contract to deal with a devil in the Valley of the Flowers near the Blue Mountains, which turned out to be a sylvan (nicknamed a 'deovel').
Rather than killing the sylvan, Geralt of Rivia tried to drive it off peacefully, showing he was not indiscriminately violent.
During the sylvan encounter, elven guerrillas surrounded Geralt of Rivia and Dandelion, and Geralt's first instinct was to negotiate for Dandelion's safety before his own.

According to Caldemeyn, ealdorman of Blaviken, seven armed people came to Blaviken including mercenaries Tavik, Nohorn, Fifteen, twins Vyr and Nimir, half-elf bandit Civril, and Renfri (called Shrike).
Renfri, known as Shrike for her habit of impaling victims, led a gang seeking vengeance against a mage she believed had wronged her.
Renfri threatened Blaviken with a 'Tridam Ultimatum,' referencing an earlier massacre where her band had killed pilgrims one by one until demands were met.
Geralt of Rivia attacked Renfri's group before they could harm anyone, resulting in a bloodbath in the Blaviken town square that killed seven people.
Geralt of Rivia and Dandelion once fished a magic amphora containing an imprisoned genie out of a river; when freed, the genie attacked Dandelion's throat instead of granting wishes.
Seeking help for Dandelion's throat injury, Geralt of Rivia traveled to Rinde and met the sorceress Yennefer for the first time.
Yennefer initially treated Geralt of Rivia as a useful tool, flirting with him while planning to use him to help capture a genie for her own power.
Yennefer cast a spell on Geralt of Rivia that put him into a trance, causing him to publicly flog several people before fainting and being jailed.
During the chaos in Rinde, the genie destroyed a quarter of the city before Geralt of Rivia used one of his wishes to win Yennefer's heart and save the city.
One year into their relationship, Geralt of Rivia left Yennefer's home in Vengerberg without warning, leaving only a letter and a bouquet of violets.
Yennefer was so enraged by Geralt of Rivia's abrupt departure that she refused to hear his name mentioned for four years afterward.
During his separation from Yennefer, Geralt of Rivia traveled to the Kingdom of Cintra on a contract that would become the most important of his life.
Geralt of Rivia was summoned to Cintra by Queen Calanthe, who feared disruption at her daughter Pavetta's birthday feast.
At Pavetta's feast, a monster called the Urcheon of Erlenwald, with the body of an armored knight and the head of a giant hedgehog, invoked the Law of Surprise to claim the right to marry Pavetta.
Geralt of Rivia suspected the Urcheon of Erlenwald was a cursed man rather than a true monster and prevented it from being killed.
The Urcheon of Erlenwald was revealed to be a southern duke named Duny, and Queen Calanthe eventually agreed to let him marry Pavetta, lifting his curse.
Grateful Duny offered Geralt of Rivia anything he desired, and Geralt invoked the Law of Surprise in return, entangling him in fate.
Calanthe was known to islanders as the Lioness of Cintra, and her death along with Duny and Pavetta's was mourned as a family tragedy by the people of the Skellige Isles.
Calanthe's second husband was Eist Tuirseach, a man from the Skellige Isles.
